c.tagline: Italy's elegant first capital, of baroque boulevards, chocolate, and an Alpine skyline.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are white and metered, with fixed surcharges at night and for luggage. Uber offers only its licensed black-car/taxi service in Turin (no UberX), so most people hail at a rank or book through Free Now or the itTaxi/appTaxi apps.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance; 113 reaches state police and 118 reaches medical emergencies directly.

avoid.reason: Caution around Porta Nuova/Porta Palazzo and San Salvario at night

hood_desc: The regal heart of the city around Piazza Castello, the Royal Palace, and the arcaded Via Roma, steps from the Mole Antonelliana and the Egyptian Museum; best for first-timers who want the landmarks and elegant historic cafes on their doorstep.

Turin's oldest quarter, a grid of narrow Roman-era streets packed with wine bars, aperitivo spots, and trattorias that come alive after dark; suits travellers who want dining and nightlife within a short stroll of the centre.

A lively, multicultural district behind Porta Nuova station bordering the leafy Parco del Valentino, known for its buzzing bars, international eateries, and young crowd; good for nightlife and more affordable stays.

One of Turin's most elegant residential areas, with tree-lined avenues, Liberty-style villas, upscale boutiques, and a well-loved open-air market; suits travellers wanting a calm, refined base near the centre.

A bohemian, student-flavoured neighbourhood by the Po river and the university, full of artisan workshops, indie cafes, and low-key bars; appeals to younger travellers and creatives after local character.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink; free 'toret' fountains flow all over the city.

transit.hours: Metro Line 1 runs roughly 5:30 AM to 10:00 PM (until about 1:00 AM Friday and Saturday), with trams and buses running until around midnight; a limited night bus network covers the late-night gap.
transit.note: GTT runs Italy's first fully automated, driverless Metro (Line 1) plus a dense network of trams and over 80 bus lines; the same ticket also covers the suburban SFM rail lines that reach the airport and nearby towns.
transit.pay: A single 'City 100' ticket is €2.00 and is valid for 100 minutes across the whole GTT network (one metro ride included); a day pass is €4.00. Tickets are sold at tobacconists, machines, and stations, and contactless tap-and-go with a bank card or phone works on new buses, trams, and metro gates.

bus: Autostazione Torino (Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, intercity/Flixbus coaches)

transit.m: SFM regional train to Torino Porta Susa (~30 min, direct)
Arriva/Sadem airport bus to Porta Nuova & Porta Susa (~45 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; a cover charge (coperto) is usually on the bill, so rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Agnolotti del plin
food.desc: Thumb-pinched Piedmontese ravioli the size of a fingernail, stuffed with three roast meats and served in their own roasting juices or on a napkin.

places.name: Madama Piola
places.note: Modern piola whose plin are widely called the best in Turin; book ahead.

places.name: Consorzio
places.note: Slow Food-minded osteria sourcing from small Piedmont producers; strong pasta list.

places.name: Porto di Savona
places.note: Arcaded trattoria open since 1863, a classic first stop for Piedmontese pasta.

food.name: Vitello tonnato
food.desc: Turin's summer antipasto: cold veal sliced paper-thin under a creamy sauce of tuna, anchovy, capers and egg. Traditionally made without mayonnaise.

places.name: Trattoria Valenza
places.note: Time-warp trattoria near Porta Palazzo doing unshowy Piedmontese classics.

places.name: Porto di Savona
places.note: Reliable, generous version on a menu of Turin standards, all day.

places.name: Da Cianci Piola Caffe
places.note: Tiny courtyard piola, cheap and always full; arrive early or queue.

food.name: Bagna cauda
food.desc: A communal pot of garlic, anchovy and olive oil kept warm over a flame, into which you dip raw and roasted vegetables. Autumn and winter only.

places.name: Le Tre Galline
places.note: Historic restaurant whose bagna cauda is the city benchmark; reserve weeks ahead.

places.name: Antiche Sere
places.note: Old-school neighbourhood osteria, no-frills and firmly Piedmontese.

places.name: Consorzio
places.note: Seasonal version with vegetables from small Piedmont growers.

food.name: Tramezzino
food.desc: The crustless triangular sandwich was invented in Turin in 1925, and the historic cafes still pile them with tuna, artichoke, egg and anchovy.

places.name: Caffe Mulassano
places.note: The 1907 belle-epoque bar where the tramezzino was created; eat standing at the marble counter.

places.name: Caffe Torino
places.note: Grand mirrored cafe on the main square with a long tramezzino counter.

places.name: Caffe San Carlo
places.note: Chandeliered 1822 salon; sandwiches, pastries and a proper aperitivo spread.

food.name: Gianduiotto
food.desc: The ingot-shaped hazelnut chocolate created in Turin when Napoleon's blockade cut off cocoa. Melts instantly; best from a small artisan maker.

places.name: Guido Gobino
places.note: Turin's most awarded chocolatier; the tourinot is a smaller, more intense gianduiotto.

places.name: Peyrano
places.note: Family chocolate house making gianduiotti by traditional extrusion since 1915.

places.name: Pasticceria Stratta
places.note: Confectioner since 1836, still selling from its original wooden cabinets.

food.name: Bonet
food.desc: Piedmont's baked pudding of chocolate, egg, amaretti crumbs and a splash of rum, turned out of a mould and pooled in caramel.

places.name: Porto di Savona
places.note: Textbook bonet to finish a plate of agnolotti; a Turin ritual.

places.name: Trattoria Valenza
places.note: Homemade dessert trolley of Piedmontese classics, bonet included.

places.name: Antiche Sere
places.note: Dense, dark, properly bitter version made in-house daily.

food.name: Bicerin
food.desc: Turin's layered glass of espresso, drinking chocolate and cream, never stirred. Invented here in the 18th century and still drunk before noon.

places.name: Al Bicerin
places.note: Serving the drink from the same tiny room since 1763; a few marble tables only.

places.name: Caffe San Carlo
places.note: Historic salon pouring a rich bicerin under the chandeliers.

places.name: Baratti & Milano
places.note: Gilded 1875 cafe and confectioner inside a glass-roofed arcade.

food.name: Vermouth di Torino
food.desc: Aromatised wine invented in Turin in 1786 and now protected by name. Drunk neat over ice with an orange twist during the evening aperitivo.

places.name: Caffe Elena
places.note: Nietzsche's old haunt; vermouth on tap and a generous free aperitivo spread.

places.name: Affini
places.note: Vermouth-led cocktail bar with Piedmontese producers behind almost every bottle.

places.name: Caffe Torino
places.note: Classic square-side terrace for a pre-dinner vermouth and olives.

landmarks: Mole Antonelliana
Turin's needle-spired icon soars 167 metres above the city, housing the superb National Cinema Museum and a glass lift to an unforgettable Alpine panorama.
Museo Egizio (Egyptian Museum)
The world's oldest Egyptian museum and finest outside Cairo displays intact tombs, papyri and the statue-lined gallery of kings in dramatically lit halls.
Palazzo Reale (Royal Palace)
The Savoy dynasty's opulent seat unfolds gilded state rooms, the Royal Armoury and Chapel of the Holy Shroud within the UNESCO-listed Royal Museums complex.
Turin Cathedral and Chapel of the Holy Shroud
The Renaissance Duomo guards Christianity's most debated relic, the Shroud of Turin, beneath Guarini's miraculously restored black-marble baroque dome.
Piazza Castello and Palazzo Madama
Turin's monumental central square surrounds Palazzo Madama, a castle-palace hybrid with Juvarra's grand baroque facade, home to the Civic Museum of Ancient Art.
Piazza San Carlo
The 'drawing room of Turin', an elegant baroque square of twin churches, arcaded historic cafés and the prancing bronze horseman Caval ëd Brons.
Basilica di Superga
Juvarra's hilltop basilica crowns Turin's skyline with royal Savoy tombs and sweeping Alpine views, reached by a charming rack tramway through the woods.
Parco del Valentino and Borgo Medievale
Turin's riverside park pairs romantic Po-side promenades with a convincing 19th-century recreation of a medieval Piedmontese village and castle.
Monte dei Cappuccini
The little church-topped hill across the Po delivers Turin's postcard view: baroque domes and the Mole silhouetted against the snow-capped Alps.
Palazzo Carignano
A rippling Baroque palace with a curved brick facade, birthplace of Italy's first king and now home to the National Museum of the Risorgimento.

train.note: Turin is Italy's rail gateway to France. Cross-border trains use Torino Porta Susa rather than Porta Nuova, and the Paris route reopened in 2025 after a long landslide closure of the Maurienne line - check it is running before you book. Domestically, Frecciarossa and Italo high-speed trains reach Milan in under an hour and Rome in about 4h10. Trenitalia opens booking around 120 days ahead and the cheap Super Economy fares go first.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches use the Torino Vittorio Emanuele II bus terminal near Porta Susa, with some services also calling at Lingotto. Coaches to Lyon take about 5 hours and Nice around 6. Bring your passport or EU ID card even though these are internal Schengen crossings.

ferry.note: Turin is inland at the foot of the Alps with no port and no navigable passenger route, so there are no ferries. The nearest sailings are from Genoa, about 1h45 south by train, where GNV and Grimaldi run to Sardinia, Sicily, Tunisia and Morocco.

half.name: Reggia di Venaria Reale
half.blurb: A Versailles-scale Savoy palace just outside Turin dazzles with Juvarra's Great Gallery, vast restored gardens and blockbuster exhibitions.
